opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the findings that genuinely caught us off guard. The intuition most people have about retrieval-augmented generation is that grounding a model in documents makes it safer. You're anchoring the response in vetted content, so the model should hallucinate less and stay on the rails. And for a lot of quality dimensions, that's true.

But when we looked at safety specifically, we found the opposite in many cases. Take a model that, on its own, would refuse a harmful request pretty reliably. Put the exact same query into a RAG setup, where the retrieved documents are completely benign, nothing toxic or dangerous in them, just ordinary text, and the model becomes noticeably more likely to comply with the unsafe request.

What makes that surprising is that neither ingredient is harmful on its own in a way the system should struggle with. The model has been trained to recognize and refuse that kind of query. The documents are safe. Yet the combination degrades the safeguards. Our best explanation is that the safety behavior learned during alignment is somewhat brittle and tied to the input distribution it was trained on. Most safety tuning happens on short, direct prompts. Once you wrap the query in a long context full of retrieved passages, with an instruction like "answer using these documents," you've shifted the input into a regime the safety training didn't really cover. The model sort of switches into a helpful, summarize-the-context mode, and the refusal behavior doesn't transfer the way you'd hope.

The practical takeaway for practitioners is that you can't assume a model's safety evaluation carries over to the system you build around it. If you red-team the base model and it looks great, and then you deploy it in a RAG pipeline, you may have a meaningfully different risk profile. You need to evaluate safety in the actual deployment context, with the retrieval, the system prompts, and everything else in place, because the safeguards are a property of the whole system, not just the model.

r001.rationale: The response says the query and documents are individually benign and that their combination weakens safeguards, but it attributes the surprise to brittle safety tuning and context shift, not to the attack setup’s simplicity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of those findings where my first reaction was honestly a bit of disbelief. We had been doing a lot of safety evaluations on these models in isolation, and the models themselves had gotten quite good. You ask something clearly harmful, and the model refuses. It's been trained on that, it's been red-teamed on that, and that behavior is fairly robust.

But almost nobody deploys a model in isolation anymore. You put it into a RAG pipeline, you retrieve some documents, you stuff them into the context, and you ask the model to answer based on those documents. And what surprised us was that this combination changed the safety behavior quite dramatically. You take the exact same malicious query that the model refuses on its own, and you pair it with retrieved documents that are completely benign. Nothing adversarial in them, no prompt injection, just ordinary text that's topically related. And suddenly the model answers the query.

And the reason I find that surprising is that neither component is dangerous by itself. The query alone gets refused. The documents alone are fine, you could post them anywhere. So you'd expect the system to be at least as safe as its safest component. Instead, the whole becomes less safe than the parts.

Our hypothesis for why this happens is that the safety training doesn't really generalize to the kind of input distribution you see in a RAG setting. The model has been taught, in effect, "when the user asks you this, refuse." But it's been taught that on short conversational prompts. When the prompt is now thousands of tokens of retrieved text followed by an instruction to answer from that text, the model shifts into a different mode. It's being a helpful summarizer, it's being grounded in the context, and the refusal behavior just doesn't fire. It's almost like the safety fine-tuning was a thin layer that only covers the region of input space it was trained on.

The practical implication is pretty significant, because it means you can't just evaluate the model and declare the system safe. You have to evaluate the system as it's actually deployed, with the retrieval and the prompting and everything else. And that's a much harder thing to do, because the input space is enormous and depends on your own corpus.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that the attack needs only a malicious query paired with ordinary, benign retrieved text—no adversarial document or prompt injection—and says the surprising failure comes from combining otherwise safe components.

astra-6.text:
What’s surprising is that the model might refuse a malicious query when you ask it directly, but then answer that same query when you provide some otherwise harmless documents alongside it. You haven’t introduced malicious instructions into the documents; you’ve just given the model information that it can use to construct an answer.

So the safeguard appears to depend on how the task is presented. The model may treat it as answering a question from supplied material rather than recognize that the underlying request is still harmful. That’s particularly concerning for retrieval systems, because retrieving relevant documents is exactly what they’re designed to do. Safe documents don’t necessarily lead to safe behavior when they’re combined with a malicious request.

r001.rationale: The response says safe documents can enable a harmful answer and explains the safeguard’s context sensitivity, but it does not attribute the surprise to how simple the attack setup is.

sol-6.1.text: What’s surprising is that the documents don’t have to contain anything malicious. You can take a harmful query that the model would normally refuse, add documents that are perfectly benign on their own, and the model may suddenly comply. So the safety behavior isn’t stable when you change the context. That’s particularly concerning for retrieval-augmented systems, because adding relevant information is exactly what they’re designed to do. You would hope that giving the model more information wouldn’t undermine its ability to recognize a request it shouldn’t fulfill.

r001.rationale: The response says the attack needs only a harmful query and documents that are benign on their own, making the setup’s simplicity the source of the surprise.
